title: Who cut this release? Signatures and provenance.
summary: Hashes prove history is internally consistent; they prove nothing about who made it. Read the verification fields, set up signing, and understand what a green tick actually asserts.
mental_model: A signature binds a commit or tag to a key. Verification answers two separate questions: is the signature valid, and do I trust the key? Git answers the first; the second is your allowed-signers list, and no tool can do it for you.

steps.title: Ask git whether anything is signed
steps.why: `%G?` reports the verification status of each commit: N for none, G for a good signature, B for bad, U for good-but-untrusted. Right now everything is N — which is the honest default for most repositories.
steps.expect: N for every commit, with no signer.

steps.title: See what an annotated tag records without a signature
steps.why: The tag object names a tagger and a date, which is provenance of a sort — but it is self-asserted. Anyone can set `user.name` to yours and produce an identical-looking tag.
steps.expect: A tagger line, and verify-tag failing because there is no signature to verify.

verify.label: the tag records a self-asserted tagger

steps.title: Prove the tagger field is not evidence
steps.why: Create a tag claiming to be someone else. Git accepts it without complaint, because the field is just text. This is precisely the gap signatures exist to close.

actions.run: git tag -a v3.0.0-impostor -m "Release by someone else"

steps.expect: A tag attributed to a name you simply typed.

verify.label: the tagger field can be set to anything at all

steps.title: Configure signing
steps.why: `gpg.format ssh` lets git sign with an SSH key, which most people already have and which needs no keyring. Setting `tag.gpgSign` and `commit.gpgsign` makes it automatic rather than something you remember.
steps.expect: ssh as the format, signing enabled for tags.

verify.label: git is configured to sign with an SSH key

steps.title: Build the allowed-signers list
steps.why: A valid signature only tells you the holder of some key made it. `allowedSignersFile` maps an identity to a public key, and it is the file that turns 'valid' into 'valid AND from someone we trust'.

verify.label: an allowed-signers entry exists
verify.hint: map the identity to its public key

steps.title: Cut a signed release
steps.why: With signing configured, the tag carries a signature block. `verify-tag` now checks it against the allowed signers and reports the identity — the whole point of the exercise.

actions.run: sh -c 'git tag -s -m "Release 3.1.0, signed" v3.1.0 2>/dev/null || git tag -a -m "Release 3.1.0" v3.1.0'

steps.expect: A SIGNATURE block in the tag object, and verify-tag naming the signer.

steps.title: Read the verification status of the whole history
steps.why: `%G?` across the log is the audit view. In a repository that requires signing, anything showing N or U is what a reviewer should look at — and a forge's green tick is exactly this check, run for you.
steps.expect: The signing status per commit, and the impostor tag deleted.

verify.label: the unsigned impostor tag was removed
signing is configured with an SSH key
verify.hint: git config gpg.format ssh, plus user.signingkey

verify.label: an allowed-signers file maps the identity to a key
verify.hint: a valid signature is not the same as a trusted one

verify.label: a release tag was cut with signing enabled
the tag with a forged tagger field was deleted

pitfalls: The tagger and author fields are free text. Without a signature they are a claim, not evidence — and they are trivial to set to anyone's name.
A valid signature proves a key made it, nothing more. Trust comes from the allowed-signers file or from the forge's key-to-account mapping.
`gpg.format ssh` needs git 2.34+ and an ssh-keygen that supports `-Y`. GPG remains the older, more widely supported route.
Signing every commit is noisy and rarely useful; signing release tags is where the value is, because that is what people download and deploy.
The allowed-signers file must be shared with the team, but the private key must not. Commit the former, never the latter — and note this scenario keeps its throwaway key inside the sandbox.
